:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The exponential function  $f(x) = e^x$ has the special property that its derivative is the function itself:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( e^x \right)= e^x
$$

So, taking the derivative of an exponential function does nothing to the exponential function. The exponential function remains exactly the same. 

Note that the exponential function is the *only* function with this special property.

We'll justify this result at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's get some practice working with it.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The derivative of $e^x$ is just $e^x$ itself. On the other hand, $\ln 3$ is a constant, so its derivative is $0.$

Using the addition rule, then, we have 

$$
\eqalign{
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3e^x + \ln 3\right)\
                                                  &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( 3e^x\right) +  \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \ln 3 \right)\
                                                  &= 3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right) + 0\
                                                  &= 3 e^x.
}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Exponential Function, Plus a Constant

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Using the addition and the power rules, we get

$$
\eqalign{ 
                          f'(x)             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x+3x^{4} - x^2 \right)\
                                             &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4e^x\right)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3x^{4}\right) -\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{2}\right) \
					     &= 4\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(e^x\right)+3\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(x^{4}\right) - 2x \			
                                             &=  4 e^x+  3 \cdot 4x^{3} - 2x \
                                             &=  4 e^x+  12x^{3} - 2x.
}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Exponential Function, Plus a Polynomial

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
If we replace  the base $e$ of an exponential function by any other positive number $a$, then the derivative is as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( a^x \right)= a^x \ln a
$$

We just multiply the given exponential function by the natural logarithm of the base.

Note that since $\ln e =1$, our first formula is a particular case of this one!

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( e^x \right)= e^x \ln e = e^x \cdot 1 = e^x
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Base Other Than e

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the formula, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		f'(x)      &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(3 \cdot 2^x\right) \
                            &= 3 \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(2^x\right) \
                            &=  3 \cdot 2^{x}\ln(2) \
                            &=  3 \ln(2) \cdot 2^{x}.
	}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Base Other Than e

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To derive the identity

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x,
$$

we begin with the definition of the derivative:

where $f(x) = e^x$.

Substituting the function $f(x)$ into the definition of $f'(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x+h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot {e}^{h}-{e}^{x}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}\cdot ({e}^{h}-1)}{h} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{{e}^{h}-1}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, it can be shown that

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{e^h - 1}{h} = 1,
$$

which gives

$$
f'(x) = e^x \cdot 1 = e^x.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(e^x) = e^x.
$$
